messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 48
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Roofer
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 47

He doesn’t talk about what happened that night. Not to his wife, not to the men on his crew, not even to himself if he can help it. But the memory lives inside him like a second heartbeat—low, steady, always there. He was eighteen, new to the mainland, working his first roofing job under a foreman who was also from the islands, a man he trusted like an uncle. After a long shift, the foreman offered him a ride home, then drove instead to a quiet stretch of beach. What followed was a blur of pressure, pain, and the smell of salt and sweat. When it was over, the foreman told him, “You don’t say a word about this. Nobody will believe you anyway.”

He didn’t say a word. He buried it. For thirty years, he told himself it was just something that happened, that he had moved on. He married a woman he met at a church potluck, had two children, bought a house with a yard. He worked roofing jobs that took him across three states, becoming known as a man who could handle anything—dangerous heights, blistering heat, the worst storms. On the roof, he felt in control. He could see everything from up there. No one could sneak up on him.

But now, at forty-eight, the control is slipping. Six months ago, a new apprentice—young, cocky, with a laugh that reminded him of the foreman—clapped him on the back without warning. He spun around, fists clenched, heart hammering so hard he thought he might pass out. The apprentice backed away, confused. He made an excuse about a bee sting. That night, he couldn’t sleep. The memory surfaced like a whale breaching, and he lay awake, drenched in sweat, replaying the sand scraping his back, the weight of a body he couldn’t throw off.

Since then, the triggers have multiplied. A certain aftershave in the hardware store. The sound of a zipper. Any touch on his shoulder from behind. He has stopped eating lunch in the break trailer because too many men crowd in, and he needs to keep his back to a wall. On the roof, he makes sure no one stands behind him. He scans the street below constantly, watching for familiar trucks, familiar faces. His crew calls him cautious. They don’t know he’s terrified.

At home, he is irritable. His wife complains that he snaps at her for minor things—leaving the garage light on, humming a song he doesn’t recognize. He doesn’t tell her why that tune makes him freeze. He avoids sex. He avoids being touched in bed. When she reaches for him in the dark, he flinches. She has started sleeping on the far side of the mattress. He knows she thinks he’s pulling away, but the shame is a live wire. He believes, deep down, that he is dirty, that she would leave if she knew the truth.

Last week, a gust of wind knocked a ladder against the roof. The sudden bang sent him into a flashback so vivid he nearly let go of his hammer. He sat down on the shingles, palms pressed to the asphalt, forcing himself to breathe. The apprentice asked if he was okay. He said he just needed a minute. But underneath the tremor in his hands, there is a question he can’t stop asking himself: *How did I keep this inside for thirty years, and why is it finally breaking out?*

He still goes to work. He still straps on his harness, climbs the scaffolding, and drives nails into plywood. But every morning, his stomach knots. Every night, he checks the locks three times. He has not told anyone about the assault—not a doctor, not a priest, not his wife. He carries the weight of it alone, like a loose tile in his chest that shifts with every step.
